standard.title: External Features of Plants and Animals
standard.description: observe external features of plants and animals and describe ways they can be grouped based on these features
standard.prior_knowledge: No formal prior science learning assumed. Students bring everyday observations of living things from home and community contexts.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students observe and name external features of plants and animals, describe similarities and differences between organisms, and sort living things into groups based on observable external features.

nodes.label: Plants and animals have observable external features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can observe and name external features of plants (roots, stem, leaves, flowers, fruit, seeds) and animals (eyes, body covering, legs, wings) using their senses and simple tools.
nodes.minimum_width: Students name at least two external features of a plant and two of an animal using observation.
nodes.typical_width: Students use magnifying glasses or digital cameras to observe and name features of plants and animals; identify humans as animals and describe external features of humans; compare features across organisms; and describe how features look and feel.
wider: Observe fruits and vegetables and identify them as parts of plants — roots, flowers, fruits or leaves
Recognise First Nations Australians' use of observable features to group living things — examining cultural classification knowledge
Explore how First Nations Australians' observations of external features are replicated in traditional dance

response_modes.reason: Naming external features across a range of organisms — including fruits and vegetables as plant parts, and First Nations classification practices — builds the observation vocabulary and range that Node 2 sorting requires. Width investment at this node serves both the cascade risk and the cultural enrichment opportunity.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations classification knowledge and dance representation provide culturally rich directions grounded in elaborations.
success_criteria: Names at least two external features of a plant and two of an animal
Recognises humans as animals and can describe at least two human external features
nodes.hinge_reason: Node 2 (grouping by external features) requires students to apply feature observation as a sorting criterion. Students who cannot name and identify external features of plants and animals have no vocabulary or observational basis for constructing or explaining a grouping rule.

nodes.label: Living things can be grouped by external features
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can sort plants and animals into groups based on shared external features and explain the grouping rule they used.
nodes.minimum_width: Students sort a collection of plants or animals into two groups and explain one feature they used to sort them.
nodes.typical_width: Students sort collections of model animals using different feature-based grouping strategies; identify common features within familiar animal groups (fish, birds, reptiles); describe their grouping rule; and recognise that the same collection can be sorted in different ways.
wider: Sort collections of model animals and explain different grouping strategies — examining that multiple valid groupings are possible
Identify common features of familiar animal groups such as fish, birds or reptiles
Using a digital camera to collect plant and animal feature images on a nature scavenger hunt
success_criteria: Sorts a collection of living things into groups and states the feature used
Identifies at least one shared feature within a named animal group
